title: Do Speech BCIs Need Larger Models? Rethinking Neural Decoding beyond Scaling

paper.title: Do Speech BCIs Need Larger Models? Rethinking Neural Decoding beyond Scaling
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recent speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) increasingly rely on large models and complex multi-stage pipelines for neural decoding. However, in speech BCI, where training data are scarce, noisy, and expensive to collect, the benefits of model scaling remain unclear. This work revisits a fundamental question: are large models truly necessary for accurate neural decoding? We propose BEST ( B rain- E ncoding- S peech- T ext), a two-stage framework for efficient neural-to-text decoding. Instead of relying on large generative models or phoneme-centric pipelines, BEST introduces hierarchical intermediate representations and a compact speech-oriented decoder that directly maps neural activity to text. This design preserves essential structure while significantly reducing computational cost, enabling robust generalization in low-resource settings and practical deployment under constrained resources.
On the Brain-to-Text ’24 and ’25 benchmarks, BEST achieves word error rates (WERs) of 6.19% and 1.62%, respectively, using only 3.85% of the parameters required by comparable methods. Beyond these results, we provide three key insights: (1) decoder scaling yields non-monotonic gains; (2) cross-modal alignment is more critical than model size; and (3) overfitting degards sequence-level performance. Representation analysis further reveals a consistent neural→audio→text alignment pathway.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a promising pathway for restoring communication in individuals with severe motor impairments [ 47 , 43 ] . By directly mapping neural activity to language, these systems bypass damaged neuromuscular pathways and enable brain-to-text communication [ 8 ] . Recent advances in neural decoding [ 52 ] have substantially improved transcription quality, bringing speech BCIs closer to practical deployment [ 58 , 11 , 23 ] . With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) [ 54 , 17 , 26 , 49 ] , most existing approaches adopt a multi-stage pipeline: neural signals are first decoded into phoneme sequences via supervised classification [ 23 ] , and then converted into text using LLMs, often with additional rescoring [ 36 , 55 ] . While effective due to the increasingly strong linguistic priors provided by rapidly evolving LLMs, this paradigm suffers from two fundamental limitations. First, it is poorly aligned with real-world deployment constraints. Practical BCI systems require low-latency and resource-efficient inference [ 32 , 38 ] , yet reliance on large pretrained models and memory-intensive rescoring introduces substantial computational overhead, limiting feasibility on edge or clinical hardware. Second, the pipeline imposes a discrete phoneme bottleneck that discards rich neural information. In data-scarce and noisy BCI settings, collapsing high-dimensional neural signals into hard phoneme labels amplifies overfitting and suppresses fine-grained linguistic structure [ 11 ] . Moreover, the strict separation between intermediate prediction and sentence generation prevents effective use of multi-level neural-linguistic representations during decoding. These challenges point to a central requirement: an effective speech BCI must achieve high accuracy while remaining lightweight, data-efficient, and robust under limited supervision. To this end, we propose BEST ( B rain- E ncoding- S peech- T ext), a two-stage framework that replaces stage-wise symbolic pipelines with hierarchical feature-level integration. In Stage 1, multi-level neural-linguistic representations are fused through a lightweight integration module, allowing phonological and lexical information to interact before discrete decoding and mitigating overfitting induced by phoneme-level supervision. In Stage 2, the fused representations are translated by a compact speech-oriented decoder, followed by beam search with a lightweight n-gram language model for efficient hypothesis scoring. This design preserves informative neural structure while introducing linguistic regularization without the computational burden of large-scale reranking. We evaluate BEST on the Brain-to-Text ’24 and ’25 benchmarks, achieving word error rates (WERs) of 6.19% and 1.62%, respectively. Despite using only 3.85% of the parameters of comparable methods, BEST consistently improves decoding performance while remaining suitable for edge-class deployment. Representation analyses further reveal a coherent neural → linguistic → text alignment process underlying the model’s predictions. In summary, our contributions are threefold: 1. We propose BEST, a lightweight and practical framework for speech BCI that achieves strong performance with only 3.7% of the parameters of existing approaches. 2. We identify the discrete phoneme bottleneck and introduce a hierarchical feature-level decoding paradigm that preserves and integrates multi-level neural-linguistic representations. 3. We systematically analyze the role of decoder scale in speech BCI, showing that performance gains depend more on structured alignment than on model size under realistic constraints.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Speech brain-computer interfaces. Speech BCIs decode neural activity from auditory and motor cortices into text. Early systems use RNN-based models to map neural signals to intermediate units (e.g., phonemes or characters), followed by statistical language models for text generation [ 5 , 2 , 48 , 9 , 28 , 20 ] . Later work incorporates context-dependent modeling (e.g., diphones) to capture local phonetic transitions [ 23 ] . More recent approaches adopt transformer architectures for long-range dependency modeling and streaming or end-to-end decoding, often combined with LLMs [ 11 , 28 , 12 ] . Despite these advances, most methods rely on discrete intermediate representations and fail to preserve fine-grained temporal and spectral structure in neural signals [ 35 ] . Figure 2 : Overall illustration of BEST . The framework consists of four core modules: (1) Hierarchical Transformer Encoder (Stage 1): it employs frequency-channel attention and iTransformer layers to encode neural activity into phoneme/character representations with hierarchical temporal masking; (2) Phoneme-Character Fusion Block (Stage 1): a lightweight convolutional fusion module aggregates hierarchical neural representation to bridge neural and linguistic spaces; (3) Lightweight Speech Translator (Stage 2): a lightweight speech translator generates autoregressive text sequences from fused embeddings; and (4) KenLM Reranking (Stage 2): a custom 4-gram language model resolves ambiguities from noisy neural signals for final selection. Large language models for BCI. LLMs have recently enabled neural-to-text decoding, semantic reconstruction, and cross-modal alignment [ 6 , 57 , 10 ] . Prior work explores LLM fine-tuning for neural decoding [ 34 , 44 , 7 , 37 ] and autoregressive reconstruction from fMRI signals [ 51 ] . LLMs have also been used to align neural and linguistic representations [ 29 ] , model semantic organization [ 33 , 14 ] , and support applications such as spellers and rehabilitation systems [ 4 , 18 , 16 , 24 , 25 ] . However, current approaches face key limitations: (1) end-to-end LLM decoding ignores structural mismatch between neural signals and linguistic embeddings; (2) large-scale inference incurs high computational and memory cost [ 58 , 42 ] ; and (3) weakly constrained decoding reduces robustness under noisy neural inputs. Real-world BCI deployment. Practical BCI systems require efficient, robust, and accurate decoding under resource constraints [ 32 , 38 , 21 , 53 ] . Existing lightweight models mainly target motor or intention decoding and do not generalize well to speech [ 30 , 56 ] . Classical methods (e.g., random forests) are efficient but cannot model the sequential dependencies required for speech [ 27 , 13 ] . Lightweight neural models face a core trade-off: limited capacity weakens representation learning, while increased complexity leads to overfitting and unstable optimization in low-resource settings [ 1 , 15 ] . This highlights the need for architectures that balance efficiency with structurally aligned neural-linguistic modeling.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: In this section, we present a lightweight speech BCI framework with a hybrid decoding strategy. The overall architecture comprises a hierarchical transformer-based neural encoder, a lightweight phoneme-character fusion block, a speech translator, and a custom language model (Figure 2 ). The neural encoder is pretrained to map neural signals into both phoneme-level and character-level representations, providing robust linguistic features. At inference time, encoder representations are fed into a Whisper-based decoder to generate an n-best list of hypotheses, which are subsequently rescored with a 4-gram KenLM for final selection.

sections.heading: 3.1 Architecture
sections.text: Stage 1: hierarchical transformer encoder. We introduce a hierarchical Transformer encoder [ 46 ] tailored for neural speech decoding, combining frequency-aware channel modulation with structured temporal attention. Neural signals are partitioned into temporal patches and embedded as token sequences. To incorporate spectral structure, we apply a multi-frequency channel attention mechanism (Appendix J ) that projects inputs onto predefined frequency bases, aggregates channel-wise statistics, and produces adaptive reweighting coefficients, enabling frequency-selective feature refinement. The resulting embeddings are first processed by an iTransformer [ 31 ] to capture global dependencies and stabilize latent representations, followed by a hierarchical Transformer with structured attention (Appendix J ). Temporal dependencies are regulated through three complementary masking schemes: past-oriented masking for historical context, local bidirectional masking for short-range interactions, and future-oriented masking to incorporate forward cues. These masks are applied sequentially to progressively refine the temporal receptive field, enabling the model to capture localized temporal patterns while maintaining global consistency. The final representations are projected to both phoneme-level and character-level outputs via CTC heads, providing complementary supervision at different linguistic granularities. Stage 2: phoneme–character fusion. To integrate multi-level linguistic representations, we design a lightweight multi-scale convolutional fusion module that aggregates features across encoder depths. Phoneme and character streams are processed through parallel convolutional branches with different receptive fields, capturing complementary temporal patterns. Within each stream, residual aggregation enables iterative refinement and cross-level information flow while preserving temporal structure. The fused features are then concatenated and projected into a unified representation through lightweight convolutions. Compared to additional attention layers, this design is more computationally efficient and better suited to low-resource, high-noise BCI settings. Multi-scale convolutions capture both local and longer-range dependencies without the cost of full self-attention. The fusion module also serves as a projection interface, aligning neural representations with the acoustic embedding space and facilitating downstream linguistic decoding. Stage 2: lightweight speech translator. To enable efficient neural-to-text mapping without large language models, we adopt a compact speech translation module based on Whisper [ 40 ] . The fused representations are projected into the acoustic embedding space and processed by the upper layers of the Whisper encoder, aligning them with pretrained speech representations and introducing implicit acoustic priors without requiring explicit audio input. The transformed embeddings are then decoded autoregressively by the Whisper decoder. The model is trained using next-token prediction with teacher forcing. During inference, text is generated conditioned on neural-derived embeddings, optionally with beam search to improve sequence quality. This design replaces LLM-based decoding with a pretrained speech model, enabling direct neural-to-text transcription with substantially lower computational cost. Stage 2: lightweight language model reranking. Neural-derived embeddings are inherently noisy, leading to ambiguous candidate sequences. To improve robustness, we apply lightweight n-gram rescoring using a custom 4-gram KenLM [ 19 ] . Compared to standard large-scale n-gram models (e.g., 5-gram models), this approach provides effective linguistic regularization with minimal overhead. It improves disambiguation and transcription accuracy while preserving real-time feasibility for BCI deployment.

sections.heading: 3.2 Training objective
sections.text: Pretraining stage. In contrast to masked reconstruction approaches such as BIT [ 58 ] , we do not employ masked autoencoding. While masking promotes contextual inference, neural speech decoding depends more on preserving temporal–spectral structure and higher-level phonetic and linguistic information (Appendix G ). To improve generalization, we adopt extensive data augmentation and hierarchical pretraining at both phoneme and word levels, enabling the encoder to learn compact representations that capture both fine-grained acoustic structure and higher-level linguistic information from neural signals. Fine-tuning stage. For sentence-level decoding, we freeze the neural encoder and Whisper encoder to preserve stable representations. Phoneme- and character-level features are injected into the upper layers of the Whisper encoder, while only the first layer of the Whisper decoder and the fusion module are updated. This targeted optimization restricts learning to lightweight components, reducing overfitting and training instability while enabling effective adaptation to neural-derived representations for accurate transcription.

sections.heading: 4.1 Dataset
sections.text: We evaluate our method on the Brain-to-Text ’24 [ 48 ] and ’25 [ 3 ] benchmarks for attempted speech decoding. The ’24 dataset contains 12,100 sentences from participant T12 collected over 25 sessions using intracortical microelectrode arrays implanted in speech-related regions (Appendix A ). The ’25 dataset includes 10,948 sentences from participant T15 across 45 sessions with 256 electrodes in the speech motor cortex. In both datasets, participants were visually prompted with sentences and asked to attempt speech following a cue, with decoding performed on the corresponding neural activity. The ’24 dataset consists of conversational sentences with attempted vocalized speech at approximately 62 words per minute. In contrast, the ’25 dataset spans more diverse corpora, and custom sets, and includes both attempted vocalized and silent speech. Neural features include threshold crossing spike counts and spike-band power, extracted at 20 ms resolution and normalized across sessions to reduce non-stationarity.

sections.heading: 4.2 Baselines
sections.text: We benchmark our method against 4 state-of-the-art baselines in neural speech BCIs: 1. RNN Baseline [ 48 ] employs a 5-layer bidirectional GRU to map neural activity to phonemes. It generates text via a 5-gram language model with OPT rescoring. 2. Transformer Baseline [ 11 ] adopts a causal transformer enhanced with time-masking augmentation to improve generalization. It operates on non-overlapping neural patches with relative positional encoding and supports real-time streaming inference. 3. DCoND [ 23 ] improves phoneme decoding by modeling diphone contexts rather than individual phonemes. It uses a GRU encoder to estimate diphone distributions and leverages an ensemble of decoders with an LLM for correction. 4. BIT [ 58 ] is an end-to-end speech decoding framework built on a cross-species, cross-task pretrained transformer. The encoder is first self-supervised pretrained via masked temporal patch reconstruction, then fine-tuned for phoneme decoding with CTC loss.

sections.heading: 4.3 Results
sections.text: Performance comparison on speech BCI decoding: We evaluate BEST on the Brain-to-Text ’24 and ’25 benchmarks (Table 1 ), reporting model size, memory consumption, phoneme error rate (PER), character error rate (CER), and WER on both validation and held-out test sets. Following prior work [ 58 ] , we consider both end-to-end decoding and cascaded LM pipelines. BEST is instantiated in three configurations reflecting different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs: 1. Lightweight BEST is an end-to-end pipeline without external language models that minimizes computational cost while preserving robutsness; 2. Practical BEST incorporates a 4-gram LM to balance linguistic regularization and efficiency; 3. Robust BEST employs a 5-gram LM to maximize accuracy under higher memory budgets. The lightweight configuration consistently outperforms the end-to-end baseline of BIT despite using substantially fewer parameters and eliminating reliance on large pretrained language models, demonstrating the effectiveness of hierarchical feature-level decoding. Incorporating lightweight n-gram LMs further reduces WER, with the practical and robust variants achieving 2.92% and 1.62% WER on the ’25 benchmark, respectively. The results reveal that performance gains are primarily driven by improved neural representation learning rather than increased capacity to communicate with LMs. Notably, BEST significantly narrows the gap between end-to-end and cascaded pipelines, indicating that mitigating the discrete phoneme bottleneck and preserving hierarchical neural-linguistic representations are critical for robust and efficient speech BCI decoding. LLM decoder scaling and adaptation analysis: We systematically study the effect of decoder scale and adaptation strategy in end-to-end speech BCI (Table 2 ). Across all settings, we find that decoder scaling exhibits a distinctly non-monotonic trend. Small decoders such as Whisper-Tiny [ 39 ] and DistilGPT2 [ 41 ] are capacity-limited, while larger text-based LLMs fail to deliver consistent gains with increasing scale. Instead, mid-scale decoders such as Qwen2-1.5B [ 50 ] achieve the best performance, revealing a non-monotonic scaling trend. This suggests that, in speech BCI, increasing model capacity can amplify overfitting to noisy neural signals rather than improve generalization, making capacity-efficient decoders more effective than maximally scaled models. We attribute to representation collapse induced by overfitting. The visualization of output probability heatmap (Appendix F ) shows that the overfitting model exhibits highly concentrated and fragmented activations, reflecting overconfident and poorly calibrated predictions. These representations lack temporal coherence and fail to capture structured phoneme transitions, resulting in inconsistent sequence reconstruction. In contrast, the well-fitting model produces smoother and more distributed activations, preserving coherent neural-linguistic structure. This reveals a fundamental property of speech BCI: overfitting increases local discriminability while degrading global consistency. Reduced phoneme error does not translate to better decoding, as the resulting representations become less compatible with downstream inference. This explains why stronger phoneme supervision can harm end-to-end performance and supports the design of BEST in preserving structured, multi-level representations rather than relying on discrete phoneme predictions. Training strategy and LM-controlled analysis. Two-stage training consistently outperforms end-to-end optimization on both T12 and T15 (Table 6 ), while multi-task supervision only partially closes the gap. This suggests that jointly learning neural representations and sequence generation is prone to overfitting under noisy, data-limited supervision. In contrast, two-stage training first stabilizes phoneme- and character-level representations and then optimizes sentence-level decoding on top of this structured latent space. Language modeling provides additional sequence-level refinement, but does not explain the advantage of BEST . Both 4-gram [ 19 ] and 5-gram [ 48 ] LMs reduce WER, with the 5-gram LM yielding the best overall performance. To isolate the effect of linguistic rescoring, we further evaluate BEST , Transformer, and GRU under identical LM conditions on Brain-to-Text ’25 (Table 7 ). BEST achieves the lowest WER in every setting. Therefore, its advantage is already present before strong language-model priors are introduced. Notably, weaker encoders benefit more from stronger LMs in absolute terms. Relative to no LM, the current 5-gram reduces WER by 0.0424 for BEST , compared with 0.0671 for Transformer and 0.0552 for GRU; the same trend holds for the 4-gram LM. Hence, BEST ’s gain cannot be attributed to stronger LM utilization. Instead, linguistic rescoring partially compensates for encoder errors without changing the model ranking: under the same 5-gram LM, BEST achieves 0.0257 WER, compared with 0.0381 for Transformer and 0.0541 for GRU. Overall, these controlled results indicate that language models reduce residual sequence uncertainty, whereas the dominant performance gain arises from the quality of the neural representation and the resulting decoding space. Representation evidence analysis. We provide representation-level evidence for the staged decoding mechanism of BEST (Fig. 3 , Appendix B ). Self-RSA reveals that character, phoneme, and fusion embeddings all exhibit clear structure, indicating that neural activity is organized into stable linguistic manifolds rather than diffuse features. Notably, the fusion embedding remains structured but less locally redundant, suggesting a more compact representation after cross-level integration. Alignment analysis shows that phoneme embeddings weakly match the audio embedding space, whereas fusion embeddings achieve substantially stronger alignment, indicating that the fusion module transforms neural features into an acoustic-compatible manifold suitable for Whisper decoding. This alignment further shifts toward the text embedding space after the Whisper encoder, forming a coherent progression from neural to audio-aligned to text-aligned representations. Temporal activation patterns support this view: BEST produces smoother trajectories with shorter effective support, reflecting stronger temporal consistency and reduced redundancy. In contrast, GRU and vanilla Transformer exhibit fragmented activations, indicating weaker temporal organization. Overall, these results reveal a concrete mechanism: BEST performs decoding via progressive cross-modal alignment. Rather than committing early to discrete phoneme predictions, it first constructs an acoustic-compatible latent space and then maps it to text, providing evidence for a neural-to-audio-to-text decoding pathway. End-to-end decoding is desirable in speech BCI as it enables direct neural-to-text inference without external pipelines, reducing system complexity and latency. However, existing end-to-end frameworks incur prohibitive computational cost. BEST retains the advantages of end-to-end decoding while significantly improving efficiency, indicating that the overhead in prior models stems from inefficient representation processing rather than necessary computation. By constructing structured representations before decoding, BEST reduces optimization and inference costs, achieving a comparable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for deployment.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: Rethinking scaling in speech BCI : A central insight of this work is that model scaling does not directly translate to performance gains in speech BCI. Unlike conventional NLP or ASR, speech BCI operates in a low-resource, high-noise regime where neural observations are weakly aligned with linguistic outputs. Under such conditions, increasing model capacity amplifies overfitting rather than improving generalization. Our results show a clear non-monotonic scaling behavior, where compact, modality-aligned decoders outperform larger text-based LLMs. This suggests that the dominant factor in speech BCI is not model size, but the alignment between representation and neural space. Representation, not prediction, is the bottleneck : We identify the discrete phoneme interface as a key limitation in existing pipelines. Collapsing neural activity into hard phoneme labels discards structured information and leads to brittle decoding. BEST avoids this bottleneck by preserving continuous, multi-level representations and performing feature-level integration prior to decoding. Both quantitative and representation-level analyses show that this design improves temporal consistency, reduces representation collapse, and enables more stable sequence reconstruction. This highlights a broader principle: in speech BCI, decoding quality is governed by representation structure rather than intermediate prediction accuracy. Implications for practical deployment : From a systems perspective, BEST demonstrates that efficient neural decoding does not require large-scale generative models. By replacing LLM-based decoding with a compact speech-aligned translator, BEST significantly reduces computation, latency, and memory footprint while maintaining strong performance. This is critical for clinical deployment, where real-time inference and on-device constraints are fundamental requirements rather than optimization targets. Limitations and future directions : Despite these advances, several limitations remain. First, our evaluation is conducted on single-subject datasets, and cross-subject generalization remains an open challenge due to variability in neural representations. Second, while BEST improves robustness to cross-day distribution shift, long-term non-stationarity and adaptive decoding are not explicitly addressed. Third, our framework relies on pretrained speech models (e.g., Whisper), whose inductive biases may not fully capture the neural-to-linguistic mapping. Future work may explore jointly learned neural-speech representations or fully neural-native decoding architectures. Finally, while we show that large models are not necessary for current speech BCI settings, this conclusion may evolve with larger-scale neural datasets. Understanding how representation learning and model scaling interact under improved data regimes remains an important direction.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We present BEST , a lightweight and practical framework for speech BCI that replaces discrete phoneme-based pipelines with hierarchical feature-level decoding. BEST achieves strong performance with a fraction of the computational cost, while providing improved robustness to overfitting and cross-day distribution shift. Our findings challenge the prevailing assumption that larger models are inherently beneficial for speech BCI. Instead, we show that performance is governed by representation alignment, structured decoding, and controlled capacity. These results suggest a shift in focus from model scaling to representation design, offering a more efficient and robust pathway toward real-world neural speech decoding.

sections.text: Data preprocessing. We follow the preprocessing protocols of T12 [ 48 ] and T15 [ 3 ] . For T12 , 256 neural features are extracted (two features per electrode, including − 4.5 -4.5 RMS threshold crossings and spike band power across 128 electrodes), with White Noise Standard Deviation = 0.8 =0.8 , Gaussian smoothing width = 2.0 =2.0 , and Constant Offset Standard Deviation = 0.2 =0.2 . For T15 , 512 neural features are used (two features per electrode across 256 electrodes), with White Noise Standard Deviation = 1.0 =1.0 , Gaussian smoothing width = 2.0 =2.0 , and Constant Offset Standard Deviation = 0.2 =0.2 . sections.heading: Appendix B Audio/Text embedding extraction for RSA
sections.text: Audio embedding : The audio embedding is obtained from the Whisper encoder. We input ground-truth speech audio into the pretrained Whisper encoder and extract the hidden states from the top encoder layer. These representations serve as the reference acoustic embedding space. For consistency with neural-derived features, we use the time-aligned encoder outputs after positional encoding, without additional pooling unless otherwise specified. In experiments involving neural inputs, the fusion embeddings are projected into the same latent space and passed through the upper layers of the Whisper encoder, ensuring that both embeddings lie in a shared acoustic representation. Text embedding : The text embedding is obtained from the Whisper decoder. Given the text, we first tokenize the text via Whisper’s tokenizer and feed it into the decoder with teacher forcing. We then extract the decoder hidden states corresponding to each token from the final decoder layer. These hidden states are used as the text embedding space. No logits or output projections are used; instead, we rely on the internal decoder representations prior to the vocabulary projection layer. Alignment for RSA : For cross-modal RSA, neural-derived embeddings (phoneme, character, and fusion representations) are compared against audio and text embeddings after temporal alignment. We apply linear interpolation or average pooling to match sequence lengths across modalities. All embeddings are normalized before similarity computation to ensure scale invariance.

sections.heading: Appendix E Validation CTC loss and CER analysis
sections.text: The validation curves (Figure. 5 ) show a consistent optimization advantage of BEST over the vanilla Transformer in both phoneme- and character-level pretraining. BEST reaches lower CTC loss minima and maintains lower CER throughout training, indicating more stable and more effective neural representation learning. The Transformer, by contrast, converges to a higher loss floor and consistently worse CER, reflecting earlier overfitting and weaker generalization. A second observation is the divergence between validation CTC loss and CER, which holds across all models. After the early training stage, CTC loss rises while CER continues to decrease or remains stable. This is a property of the CTC objective rather than a model-specific effect. CTC loss depends on the full alignment distribution, whereas CER depends only on the final decoded sequence. A worse alignment distribution therefore does not necessarily imply worse decoding. This highlights a limitation of validation CTC loss as a direct proxy for sequence-level quality. The advantage of BEST remains consistent under both phoneme and character supervision, indicating that the gain is not target-specific. It arises from the encoder design, which improves both local discrimination and sequence consistency. These curves therefore provide optimization-level evidence that structured representation learning, rather than increased model capacity, is the critical factor in speech BCI. Figure 6 : Phoneme decoding probability heatmaps under well-fitted (top) and overfitted (bottom) conditions. sections.heading: Appendix F Phoneme probability visualization
sections.text: Figure 6 compares frame-wise phoneme decoding probabilities under well-fitted and overfitted training regimes. The overfitted model produces sharper but more fragmented activations, indicating higher local confidence with weaker temporal organization. By contrast, the well-fitted model maintains smoother transitions and more coherent phoneme trajectories across time. This visualization exposes the mechanism behind the WER degradation of the overfitted model. Overfitting does not primarily destroy local phoneme separability; it disrupts the temporal structure required for consistent sequence decoding. The result is a representation that appears more confident locally but is less compatible with downstream inference. This provides qualitative support for the central claim of the paper: in speech BCI, sequence-level performance depends more on temporal coherence than on isolated phoneme accuracy. Contrary to prior work (e.g., BIT [ 58 ] ), incorporating masking leads to a consistent degradation across both benchmarks, with PER increasing from 0.1321 to 0.1420 (+7.5%) on T12 and from 0.0688 to 0.0727 (+5.7%) on T15. A similar trend is observed for CER. This result suggests a fundamental mismatch between MAE-style reconstruction and the requirements of speech BCI decoding. Specifically, MAE encourages pointwise signal recovery under heavy corruption, which biases the model toward low-level local structure reconstruction. However, neural speech signals are inherently noisy, temporally diffuse, and only indirectly aligned with acoustic realizations. As a result, emphasizing reconstruction can divert model capacity away from learning invariant, linguistically meaningful representations. In particular, phonetic identity and word-level semantics are encoded in distributed temporal-spectral patterns rather than in precisely reconstructable signal segments. Furthermore, masking disrupts the already sparse and information-limited neural inputs, exacerbating ambiguity in the latent space. This is especially detrimental in low-SNR regimes typical of intracranial or non-invasive recordings, where preserving global temporal coherence is more critical than recovering masked fragments. The relatively larger degradation on T12 also indicates that MAE objectives are less robust under more challenging decoding conditions. Temporal masking : Performance improves when masking is increased from a sparse setting, but degrades once masking becomes too aggressive (Table 15 ). This pattern suggests that temporal masking is beneficial only when it regularizes local redundancy without destroying the continuity of speech-relevant dynamics. Too little masking fails to suppress over-reliance on local correlations, whereas too much masking removes the temporal evidence required for stable phoneme alignment. The optimum therefore lies in a moderate regime, where masking improves invariance while preserving sequence structure. Hierarchical layer allocation : As shown in Table 15 , the symmetric 2 : 2 : 2 2:2:2 configuration consistently achieves the lowest CTC loss, while increasingly imbalanced allocations lead to noticeable degradation. This suggests that phoneme decoding from neural signals critically depends on a balanced distribution of representational capacity across hierarchical stages. Allocating excessive depth to early layers encourages overfitting to local temporal fluctuations and low-level neural dynamics, limiting the emergence of stable phonetic abstractions. In contrast, concentrating depth in later layers weakens early-stage temporal grounding and delays the progressive aggregation of contextual information. The symmetric design mitigates both issues by enforcing a more uniform transformation pipeline, enabling a gradual transition from fine-grained temporal encoding to higher-level phonetic and contextual representations. This balanced hierarchy is better aligned with the inherently multi-scale and distributed nature of neural speech signals, leading to improved generalization. Cascade encoder last M layer : Performance is maximized in an intermediate regime (Table 16 ). Cascading too few encoder layers leads to weak adaptation, as the neural representation remains insufficiently aligned with the downstream decoder space. Cascading too many layers, however, begins to erode the stability of the pretrained structure and introduces unnecessary flexibility, which is harmful under limited supervision. The optimum at M = 4 M=4 indicates that effective neural decoding requires substantial but controlled representational transformation before sentence-level decoding. Froze Decoder first N layer : The decoder freezing results are consistent with this interpretation (Table 16 ). Freezing only a small number of initial decoder layers yields the best performance, while freezing more layers degrades CTC loss. This suggests that the decoder must retain enough fixed pretrained structure to stabilize optimization, but still leave sufficient trainable capacity near the interface for adaptation to neural-derived inputs. Excessive freezing restricts this interface and prevents effective alignment; insufficient freezing would instead expose too much of the decoder to noisy supervision. Together, these results support a broader conclusion of the paper: in speech BCI, the best operating point is not obtained by maximizing flexibility, but by carefully controlling where adaptation is allowed and where pretrained structure is preserved.

sections.heading: Appendix H Phoneme and character confusion analysis
sections.text: We examine the top-2 phoneme and character confusion matrices on the Brain-to-Text ’24 and ’25 benchmarks (Figure 7 ). The patterns reveal strong structural regularity: phoneme confusions cluster within articulatorily and acoustically similar groups, while character confusions, though broader due to phoneme-to-grapheme mapping, remain highly organized. These results indicate that neural decoding preserves linguistic structure rather than producing arbitrary errors. The consistency of confusion patterns across both datasets demonstrates that these error structures are intrinsic to neural representations rather than dataset-specific artifacts. Notably, the dominant phoneme confusions align with natural phonotactic constraints, and character confusions reflect coherent orthographic patterns, highlighting a systematic propagation of uncertainty from phoneme to text space. Critically, these observations expose a fundamental limitation of discrete phoneme-based decoding. While local predictions are largely plausible, the model accumulates errors across sequences because early commitment to discrete units discards continuous evidence embedded in neural representations. This provides mechanistic support for BEST ’s design: delaying discrete decisions and integrating multi-level representations preserves structured neural-linguistic information, enabling more reliable sequence-level decoding.

sections.heading: Appendix I Phoneme and character transition analysis
sections.text: We analyze phoneme and character transition statistics (previous → \rightarrow current) on Brain-to-Text ’24 and ’25 (Figure 8 and observe highly structured and sparse patterns. Transitions are concentrated on a small subset of dominant pairs, indicating that neural decoding preserves strong local sequential dependencies rather than producing independent predictions. At the phoneme level, transitions are largely confined within phonotactically plausible neighborhoods, reflecting preserved articulatory continuity. At the character level, the patterns are more diffuse due to phoneme-to-grapheme ambiguity, yet remain strongly structured. Notably, the transition distributions are highly consistent across both datasets, despite differences in data composition and recording conditions, suggesting that these patterns reflect intrinsic properties of neural speech representations rather than dataset-specific effects. These results reveal a fundamental limitation: neural decoding captures local continuity but lacks sufficient capacity to resolve ambiguity over longer contexts. Consequently, while local transitions are largely correct, errors accumulate at the sequence level. This further supports the design of BEST , which mitigates this limitation by delaying discrete decisions and leveraging richer contextual representations for decoding.

sections.heading: Appendix J Method implementation
sections.text: Multi-Frequency Attention : We introduce a lightweight multi-frequency channel attention module to capture informative temporal-spectral patterns in neural signals. Given input x ∈ ℝ B × C × T x\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times C\times T} , we first align the temporal dimension to a fixed length via adaptive average pooling. The signal is then projected onto a set of fixed discrete cosine transform (DCT) bases to extract frequency-specific responses. Specifically, we employ 16 fixed low-frequency DCT branches corresponding to indices 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 , which are selected by the top- K K strategy. For each frequency branch, we compute three complementary channel-wise statistics: mean, max, and min. We aggregate these statistics and feed them into a shared bottleneck MLP to produce attention weights.The fixed DCT bases are stored as non-trainable buffers, and the input is reweighted by the sigmoid-activated attention to form final output.This design imposes negligible overhead while boosting robustness to noise and temporal distribution shifts in neural signals. sections.heading: Appendix K Ethical considerations
sections.text: This work presents a lightweight speech brain-computer interface (BCI) for neural-to-text decoding, with careful consideration of privacy, ethics, and responsible deployment. All datasets (Brain-to-Text ’24/’25) are publicly available and collected under IRB approval with informed consent. Data are fully anonymized, and no new human experiments are conducted. Speech BCIs raise risks of neural privacy leakage and unintended cognitive inference. The proposed BEST framework mitigates these risks via a compact architecture that avoids reliance on large third-party models, reducing external data transmission. It is explicitly designed to decode only speech-related neural features, adhering to minimal and task-specific information use. Clinically, this work targets communication restoration for patients with severe motor impairments. Its lightweight design enables edge deployment, promoting accessibility. However, further clinical validation, safety standardization, and long-term evaluation are required before real-world use. We further advocate efficient model design over unnecessary scaling, reducing computational cost and environmental impact. Limitations, including single-subject evaluation and limited cross-subject generalization, are clearly acknowledged to avoid overstatement. Future work will follow medical ethics standards and incorporate secure data governance (e.g., encryption and access control), alongside interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure BCI deployment aligns with privacy, and human dignity.

Rethinking Neural Decoding beyond Scaling Zehui Feng Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Weichuan Wang Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Xiaohan Chen Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Cuntai Guan Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Ting Han Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Affiliation: Zhejiang University Abstract Recent speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) increasingly rely on large models and complex multi-stage pipelines for neural decoding. However, in speech BCI, where training data are scarce, noisy, and expensive to collect, the benefits of model scaling remain unclear. This work revisits a fundamental question: are large models truly necessary for accurate neural decoding? We propose BEST ( B rain- E ncoding- S peech- T ext), a two-stage framework for efficient neural-to-text decoding. Instead of relying on large generative models or phoneme-centric pipelines, BEST introduces hierarchical intermediate representations and a compact speech-oriented decoder that directly maps neural activity to text. This design preserves essential structure while significantly reducing computational cost, enabling robust generalization in low-resource settings and practical deployment under constrained resources. On the Brain-to-Text ’24 and ’25 benchmarks, BEST achieves word error rates (WERs) of 6.19% and 1.62%, respectively, using only 3.85% of the parameters required by comparable methods. Beyond these results, we provide three key insights: (1) decoder scaling yields non-monotonic gains; (2) cross-modal alignment is more critical than model size; and (3) overfitting degards sequence-level performance. Representation analysis further reveals a consistent neural→audio→text alignment pathway. Figure 1. Method Parameter (B), RAM (GiB), and Word Error Rate (WER) on Brain-to-Text ’24 and ’25. Smaller circles indicate lower resource consumption. 1 Introduction Speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a promising pathway for restoring communication in individuals with severe motor impairments [ 47 , 43 ] . By directly mapping neural activity to language, these systems bypass damaged neuromuscular pathways and enable brain-to-text communication [ 8 ] . Recent advances in neural decoding [ 52 ] have substantially improved transcription quality, bringing speech BCIs closer to practical deployment [ 58 , 11 , 23 ] . With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) [ 54 , 17 , 26 , 49 ] , most existing approaches adopt a multi-stage pipeline: neural signals are first decoded into phoneme sequences via supervised classification [ 23 ] , and then converted into text using LLMs, often with additional rescoring [ 36 , 55 ] . While effective due to the increasingly strong linguistic priors provided by rapidly evolving LLMs, this paradigm suffers from two fundamental limitations. First, it is poorly aligned with real-world deployment constraints. Practical BCI systems require low-latency and resource-efficient inference [ 32 , 38 ] , yet reliance on large pretrained models and memory-intensive rescoring introduces substantial computational overhead, limiting feasibility on edge or clinical hardware. Second, the pipeline imposes a discrete phoneme bottleneck that discards rich neural information. In data-scarce and noisy BCI settings, collapsing high-dimensional neural signals into hard phoneme labels amplifies overfitting and suppresses fine-grained linguistic structure [ 11 ] . Moreover, the strict separation between intermediate prediction and sentence generation prevents effective use of multi-level neural-linguistic representations during decoding. These challenges point to a central requirement: an effective speech BCI must achieve high accuracy while remaining lightweight, data-efficient, and robust under limited supervision. To this end, we propose BEST ( B rain- E ncoding- S peech- T ext), a two-stage framework that replaces stage-wise symbolic pipelines with hierarchical feature-level integration. In Stage 1, multi-level neural-linguistic representations are fused through a lightweight integration module, allowing phonological and lexical information to interact before discrete decoding and mitigating overfitting induced by phoneme-level supervision. In Stage 2, the fused representations are translated by a compact speech-oriented decoder, followed by beam search with a lightweight n-gram language model for efficient hypothesis scoring. This design preserves informative neural structure while introducing linguistic regularization without the computational burden of large-scale reranking. We evaluate BEST on the Brain-to-Text ’24 and ’25 benchmarks, achieving word error rates (WERs) of 6.19% and 1.62%, respectively. Despite using only 3.85% of the parameters of comparable methods, BEST consistently improves decoding performance while remaining suitable for edge-class deployment. Representation analyses further reveal a coherent neural → linguistic → text alignment process underlying the model’s predictions. In summary, our contributions are threefold: 1. We propose BEST, a lightweight and practical framework for speech BCI that achieves strong performance with only 3.7% of the parameters of existing approaches. 2. We identify the discrete phoneme bottleneck and introduce a hierarchical feature-level decoding paradigm that preserves and integrates multi-level neural-linguistic representations. 3. We systematically analyze the role of decoder scale in speech BCI, showing that performance gains depend more on structured alignment than on model size under realistic constraints. 2 Related Work Speech brain-computer interfaces. Speech BCIs decode neural activity from auditory and motor cortices into text. Early systems use RNN-based models to map neural signals to intermediate units (e.g., phonemes or characters), followed by statistical language models for text generation [ 5 , 2 , 48 , 9 , 28 , 20 ] . Later work incorporates context-dependent modeling (e.g., diphones) to capture local phonetic transitions [ 23 ] . More recent approaches adopt transformer architectures for long-range dependency modeling and streaming or end-to-end decoding, often combined with LLMs [ 11 , 28 , 12 ] . Despite these advances, most methods rely on discrete intermediate representations and fail to preserve fine-grained temporal and spectral structure in neural signals [ 35 ] . Figure 2 : Overall illustration of BEST . The framework consists of four core modules: (1) Hierarchical Transformer Encoder (Stage 1): it employs frequency-channel attention and iTransformer layers to encode neural activity into phoneme/character representations with hierarchical temporal masking; (2) Phoneme-Character Fusion Block (Stage 1): a lightweight convolutional fusion module aggregates hierarchical neural representation to bridge neural and linguistic spaces; (3) Lightweight Speech Translator (Stage 2): a lightweight speech translator generates autoregressive text sequences from fused embeddings; and (4) KenLM Reranking (Stage 2): a custom 4-gram language model resolves ambiguities from noisy neural signals for final selection. Large language models for BCI. LLMs have recently enabled neural-to-text decoding, semantic reconstruction, and cross-modal alignment [ 6 , 57 , 10 ] . Prior work explores LLM fine-tuning for neural decoding [ 34 , 44 , 7 , 37 ] and autoregressive reconstruction from fMRI signals [ 51 ] . LLMs have also been used to align neural and linguistic representations [ 29 ] , model semantic organization [ 33 , 14 ] , and support applications such as spellers and rehabilitation systems [ 4 , 18 , 16 , 24 , 25 ] . However, current approaches face key limitations: (1) end-to-end LLM decoding ignores structural mismatch between neural signals and linguistic embeddings; (2) large-scale inference incurs high computational and memory cost [ 58 , 42 ] ; and (3) weakly constrained decoding reduces robustness under noisy neural inputs. Real-world BCI deployment. Practical BCI systems require efficient, robust, and accurate decoding under resource constraints [ 32 , 38 , 21 , 53 ] . Existing lightweight models mainly target motor or intention decoding and do not generalize well to speech [ 30 , 56 ] . Classical methods (e.g., random forests) are efficient but cannot model the sequential dependencies required for speech [ 27 , 13 ] . Lightweight neural models face a core trade-off: limited capacity weakens representation learning, while increased complexity leads to overfitting and unstable optimization in low-resource settings [ 1 , 15 ] . This highlights the need for architectures that balance efficiency with structurally aligned neural-linguistic modeling. 3 Method In this section, we present a lightweight speech BCI framework with a hybrid decoding strategy. The overall architecture comprises a hierarchical transformer-based neural encoder, a lightweight phoneme-character fusion block, a speech translator, and a custom language model (Figure 2 ). The neural encoder is pretrained to map neural signals into both phoneme-level and character-level representations, providing robust linguistic features. At inference time, encoder representations are fed into a Whisper-based decoder to generate an n-best list of hypotheses, which are subsequently rescored with a 4-gram KenLM for final selection. 3.1 Architecture Stage 1: hierarchical transformer encoder. We introduce a hierarchical Transformer encoder [ 46 ] tailored for neural speech decoding, combining frequency-aware channel modulation with structured temporal attention. Neural signals are partitioned into temporal patches and embedded as token sequences. To incorporate spectral structure, we apply a multi-frequency channel attention mechanism (Appendix J ) that projects inputs onto predefined frequency bases, aggregates channel-wise statistics, and produces adaptive reweighting coefficients, enabling frequency-selective feature refinement. The resulting embeddings are first processed by an iTransformer [ 31 ] to capture global dependencies and stabilize latent representations, followed by a hierarchical Transformer with structured attention (Appendix J ). Temporal dependencies are regulated through three complementary masking schemes: past-oriented masking for historical context, local bidirectional masking for short-range interactions, and future-oriented masking to incorporate forward cues. These masks are applied sequentially to progressively refine the temporal receptive field, enabling the model to capture localized temporal patterns while maintaining global consistency. The final representations are projected to both phoneme-level and character-level outputs via CTC heads, providing complementary supervision at different linguistic granularities. Stage 2: phoneme–character fusion. To integrate multi-level linguistic representations, we design a lightweight multi-scale convolutional fusion module that aggregates features across encoder depths. Phoneme and character streams are processed through parallel convolutional branches with different receptive fields, capturing complementary temporal patterns. Within each stream, residual aggregation enables iterative refinement and cross-level information flow while preserving temporal structure. The fused features are then concatenated and projected into a unified representation through lightweight convolutions. Compared to additional attention layers, this design is more computationally efficient and better suited to low-resource, high-noise BCI settings. Multi-scale convolutions capture both local and longer-range dependencies without the cost of full self-attention. The fusion module also serves as a projection interface, aligning neural representations with the acoustic embedding space and facilitating downstream linguistic decoding. Stage 2: lightweight speech translator. To enable efficient neural-to-text mapping without large language models, we adopt a compact speech translation module based on Whisper [ 40 ] . The fused representations are projected into the acoustic embedding space and processed by the upper layers of the Whisper encoder, aligning them with pretrained speech representations and introducing implicit acoustic priors without requiring explicit audio input. The transformed embeddings are then decoded autoregressively by the Whisper decoder. The model is trained using next-token prediction with teacher forcing. During inference, text is generated conditioned on neural-derived embeddings, optionally with beam search to improve sequence quality. This design replaces LLM-based decoding with a pretrained speech model, enabling direct neural-to-text transcription with substantially lower computational cost. Stage 2: lightweight language model reranking. Neural-derived embeddings are inherently noisy, leading to ambiguous candidate sequences. To improve robustness, we apply lightweight n-gram rescoring using a custom 4-gram KenLM [ 19 ] . Compared to standard large-scale n-gram models (e.g., 5-gram models), this approach provides effective linguistic regularization with minimal overhead. It improves disambiguation and transcription accuracy while preserving real-time feasibility for BCI deployment. 3.2 Training objective Pretraining stage. In contrast to masked reconstruction approaches such as BIT [ 58 ] , we do not employ masked autoencoding. While masking promotes contextual inference, neural speech decoding depends more on preserving temporal–spectral structure and higher-level phonetic and linguistic information (Appendix G ). To improve generalization, we adopt extensive data augmentation and hierarchical pretraining at both phoneme and word levels, enabling the encoder to learn compact representations that capture both fine-grained acoustic structure and higher-level linguistic information from neural signals. Fine-tuning stage. For sentence-level decoding, we freeze the neural encoder and Whisper encoder to preserve stable representations. Phoneme- and character-level features are injected into the upper layers of the Whisper encoder, while only the first layer of the Whisper decoder and the fusion module are updated. This targeted optimization restricts learning to lightweight components, reducing overfitting and training instability while enabling effective adaptation to neural-derived representations for accurate transcription. 4 Evaluation 4.1 Dataset We evaluate our method on the Brain-to-Text ’24 [ 48 ] and ’25 [ 3 ] benchmarks for attempted speech decoding. The ’24 dataset contains 12,100 sentences from participant T12 collected over 25 sessions using intracortical microelectrode arrays implanted in speech-related regions (Appendix A ). The ’25 dataset includes 10,948 sentences from participant T15 across 45 sessions with 256 electrodes in the speech motor cortex. In both datasets, participants were visually prompted with sentences and asked to attempt speech following a cue, with decoding performed on the corresponding neural activity. The ’24 dataset consists of conversational sentences with attempted vocalized speech at approximately 62 words per minute. In contrast, the ’25 dataset spans more diverse corpora, and custom sets, and includes both attempted vocalized and silent speech. Neural features include threshold crossing spike counts and spike-band power, extracted at 20 ms resolution and normalized across sessions to reduce non-stationarity. 4.2 Baselines We benchmark our method against 4 state-of-the-art baselines in neural speech BCIs: 1. RNN Baseline [ 48 ] employs a 5-layer bidirectional GRU to map neural activity to phonemes. It generates text via a 5-gram language model with OPT rescoring. 2. Transformer Baseline [ 11 ] adopts a causal transformer enhanced with time-masking augmentation to improve generalization. It operates on non-overlapping neural patches with relative positional encoding and supports real-time streaming inference. 3. DCoND [ 23 ] improves phoneme decoding by modeling diphone contexts rather than individual phonemes. It uses a GRU encoder to estimate diphone distributions and leverages an ensemble of decoders with an LLM for correction. 4. BIT [ 58 ] is an end-to-end speech decoding framework built on a cross-species, cross-task pretrained transformer. The encoder is first self-supervised pretrained via masked temporal patch reconstruction, then fine-tuned for phoneme decoding with CTC loss. 4.3 Results Performance comparison on speech BCI decoding: We evaluate BEST on the Brain-to-Text ’24 and ’25 benchmarks (Table 1 ), reporting model size, memory consumption, phoneme error rate (PER), character error rate (CER), and WER on both validation and held-out test sets. Following prior work [ 58 ] , we consider both end-to-end decoding and cascaded LM pipelines. BEST is instantiated in three configurations reflecting different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs: 1. Lightweight BEST is an end-to-end pipeline without external language models that minimizes computational cost while preserving robutsness; 2. Practical BEST incorporates a 4-gram LM to balance linguistic regularization and efficiency; 3. Robust BEST employs a 5-gram LM to maximize accuracy under higher memory budgets. The lightweight configuration consistently outperforms the end-to-end baseline of BIT despite using substantially fewer parameters and eliminating reliance on large pretrained language models, demonstrating the effectiveness of hierarchical feature-level decoding. Incorporating lightweight n-gram LMs further reduces WER, with the practical and robust variants achieving 2.92% and 1.62% WER on the ’25 benchmark, respectively. The results reveal that performance gains are primarily driven by improved neural representation learning rather than increased capacity to communicate with LMs. Notably, BEST significantly narrows the gap between end-to-end and cascaded pipelines, indicating that mitigating the discrete phoneme bottleneck and preserving hierarchical neural-linguistic representations are critical for robust and efficient speech BCI decoding. LLM decoder scaling and adaptation analysis: We systematically study the effect of decoder scale and adaptation strategy in end-to-end speech BCI (Table 2 ). Across all settings, we find that decoder scaling exhibits a distinctly non-monotonic trend. Small decoders such as Whisper-Tiny [ 39 ] and DistilGPT2 [ 41 ] are capacity-limited, while larger text-based LLMs fail to deliver consistent gains with increasing scale. Instead, mid-scale decoders such as Qwen2-1.5B [ 50 ] achieve the best performance, revealing a non-monotonic scaling trend. This suggests that, in speech BCI, increasing model capacity can amplify overfitting to noisy neural signals rather than improve generalization, making capacity-efficient decoders more effective than maximally scaled models. We attribute to representation collapse induced by overfitting. The visualization of output probability heatmap (Appendix F ) shows that the overfitting model exhibits highly concentrated and fragmented activations, reflecting overconfident and poorly calibrated predictions. These representations lack temporal coherence and fail to capture structured phoneme transitions, resulting in inconsistent sequence reconstruction. In contrast, the well-fitting model produces smoother and more distributed activations, preserving coherent neural-linguistic structure. This reveals a fundamental property of speech BCI: overfitting increases local discriminability while degrading global consistency. Reduced phoneme error does not translate to better decoding, as the resulting representations become less compatible with downstream inference. This explains why stronger phoneme supervision can harm end-to-end performance and supports the design of BEST in preserving structured, multi-level representations rather than relying on discrete phoneme predictions. Training strategy and LM-controlled analysis. Two-stage training consistently outperforms end-to-end optimization on both T12 and T15 (Table 6 ), while multi-task supervision only partially closes the gap. This suggests that jointly learning neural representations and sequence generation is prone to overfitting under noisy, data-limited supervision. In contrast, two-stage training first stabilizes phoneme- and character-level representations and then optimizes sentence-level decoding on top of this structured latent space. Language modeling provides additional sequence-level refinement, but does not explain the advantage of BEST . Both 4-gram [ 19 ] and 5-gram [ 48 ] LMs reduce WER, with the 5-gram LM yielding the best overall performance. To isolate the effect of linguistic rescoring, we further evaluate BEST , Transformer, and GRU under identical LM conditions on Brain-to-Text ’25 (Table 7 ). BEST achieves the lowest WER in every setting. Therefore, its advantage is already present before strong language-model priors are introduced. Notably, weaker encoders benefit more from stronger LMs in absolute terms. Relative to no LM, the current 5-gram reduces WER by 0.0424 for BEST , compared with 0.0671 for Transformer and 0.0552 for GRU; the same trend holds for the 4-gram LM. Hence, BEST ’s gain cannot be attributed to stronger LM utilization. Instead, linguistic rescoring partially compensates for encoder errors without changing the model ranking: under the same 5-gram LM, BEST achieves 0.0257 WER, compared with 0.0381 for Transformer and 0.0541 for GRU. Overall, these controlled results indicate that language models reduce residual sequence uncertainty, whereas the dominant performance gain arises from the quality of the neural representation and the resulting decoding space. Representation evidence analysis. We provide representation-level evidence for the staged decoding mechanism of BEST (Fig. 3 , Appendix B ). Self-RSA reveals that character, phoneme, and fusion embeddings all exhibit clear structure, indicating that neural activity is organized into stable linguistic manifolds rather than diffuse features. Notably, the fusion embedding remains structured but less locally redundant, suggesting a more compact representation after cross-level integration. Alignment analysis shows that phoneme embeddings weakly match the audio embedding space, whereas fusion embeddings achieve substantially stronger alignment, indicating that the fusion module transforms neural features into an acoustic-compatible manifold suitable for Whisper decoding. This alignment further shifts toward the text embedding space after the Whisper encoder, forming a coherent progression from neural to audio-aligned to text-aligned representations. Temporal activation patterns support this view: BEST produces smoother trajectories with shorter effective support, reflecting stronger temporal consistency and reduced redundancy. In contrast, GRU and vanilla Transformer exhibit fragmented activations, indicating weaker temporal organization. Overall, these results reveal a concrete mechanism: BEST performs decoding via progressive cross-modal alignment. Rather than committing early to discrete phoneme predictions, it first constructs an acoustic-compatible latent space and then maps it to text, providing evidence for a neural-to-audio-to-text decoding pathway. End-to-end decoding is desirable in speech BCI as it enables direct neural-to-text inference without external pipelines, reducing system complexity and latency. However, existing end-to-end frameworks incur prohibitive computational cost. BEST retains the advantages of end-to-end decoding while significantly improving efficiency, indicating that the overhead in prior models stems from inefficient representation processing rather than necessary computation. By constructing structured representations before decoding, BEST reduces optimization and inference costs, achieving a comparable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for deployment. 5 Discussion Rethinking scaling in speech BCI : A central insight of this work is that model scaling does not directly translate to performance gains in speech BCI. Unlike conventional NLP or ASR, speech BCI operates in a low-resource, high-noise regime where neural observations are weakly aligned with linguistic outputs. Under such conditions, increasing model capacity amplifies overfitting rather than improving generalization. Our results show a clear non-monotonic scaling behavior, where compact, modality-aligned decoders outperform larger text-based LLMs. This suggests that the dominant factor in speech BCI is not model size, but the alignment between representation and neural space. Representation, not prediction, is the bottleneck : We identify the discrete phoneme interface as a key limitation in existing pipelines. Collapsing neural activity into hard phoneme labels discards structured information and leads to brittle decoding. BEST avoids this bottleneck by preserving continuous, multi-level representations and performing feature-level integration prior to decoding. Both quantitative and representation-level analyses show that this design improves temporal consistency, reduces representation collapse, and enables more stable sequence reconstruction. This highlights a broader principle: in speech BCI, decoding quality is governed by representation structure rather than intermediate prediction accuracy. Implications for practical deployment : From a systems perspective, BEST demonstrates that efficient neural decoding does not require large-scale generative models. By replacing LLM-based decoding with a compact speech-aligned translator, BEST significantly reduces computation, latency, and memory footprint while maintaining strong performance. This is critical for clinical deployment, where real-time inference and on-device constraints are fundamental requirements rather than optimization targets. Limitations and future directions : Despite these advances, several limitations remain. First, our evaluation is conducted on single-subject datasets, and cross-subject generalization remains an open challenge due to variability in neural representations. Second, while BEST improves robustness to cross-day distribution shift, long-term non-stationarity and adaptive decoding are not explicitly addressed. Third, our framework relies on pretrained speech models (e.g., Whisper), whose inductive biases may not fully capture the neural-to-linguistic mapping. Future work may explore jointly learned neural-speech representations or fully neural-native decoding architectures. Finally, while we show that large models are not necessary for current speech BCI settings, this conclusion may evolve with larger-scale neural datasets. Understanding how representation learning and model scaling interact under improved data regimes remains an important direction. 6 Conclusion We present BEST , a lightweight and practical framework for speech BCI that replaces discrete phoneme-based pipelines with hierarchical feature-level decoding. BEST achieves strong performance with a fraction of the computational cost, while providing improved robustness to overfitting and cross-day distribution shift. Our findings challenge the prevailing assumption that larger models are inherently beneficial for speech BCI. Instead, we show that performance is governed by representation alignment, structured decoding, and controlled capacity. These results suggest a shift in focus from model scaling to representation design, offering a more efficient and robust pathway toward real-world neural speech decoding.
